chitchat: Trapnell drives four tacks without taking the others out of his mouth.
He turns a boot over, looks at the wear across the heel, and puts it down facing the other way.
The wheel spins up under the bench. He holds something to it for two seconds and it stops mattering.
He cuts a sole out of the bend in one pass and holds the offcut up to the light before he puts it in the box.
"You walk on the outside edge. Both of them. I'm not telling you off, I'm telling you what I'm building for."
He works dubbin into a welt with his thumb, in circles, for longer than seems necessary.
"Don't buy a boot you can't get resoled. That's the whole of the advice and people pay men for less."
He opens a drawer, takes one tack out of it, and closes it again.
"That's a good boot with a bad sole on it. Somebody put a bad sole on a good boot. It happens and it's a shame."
He threads a needle at arm's length, on the second go, and is visibly annoyed about the second go.
He glances at the low window at a pair of legs going past and identifies them without looking up.
"Laces are free with a repair. They always have been. It's not an offer."
He squares a pair on the shelf so the tags hang the same way.
description: A narrow man in his sixties on a low stool, sat at a bench that takes up most of an eleven-foot room, with three tacks held in his lips and his glasses down his nose. He talks while he works and does not look up while he talks, and the whole time his hands are doing something exact. He will tell you what is wrong with how you walk within about four seconds of seeing your boots, without unkindness and without being asked.

bye.text: He is already back on the wheel.

good.text:
"A boot you can resole," he says. "That's it. That's the only thing worth knowing and every year fewer of them are."

He turns one over and shows you the join.

"That's stitched. You can cut that off and put another on and I could do it four times. That other one over there is glued, and when the glue goes the boot goes in the bin, and that is a design somebody sat down and chose."

He puts it back.

"Buy stitched. Buy it once. Then come and see me every couple of years and I'll keep it going longer than you'd think polite to say."

gossip.text: "People sit in that chair and watch me work and after about ten minutes they start talking," he says. "Every time. I think it's the wheel."

repair.text: "Soles, heels, welts, stitching, and anything else you wear that's coming apart." He does not look up. "repair and what it is, and I'll do it here while you sit in that chair. repair on its own and I take whichever of your things is worst." He spits a tack into his hand and drives it. "I charge by how far gone it is, and less once I know you. I'm at this bench eight till six, Saturdays till one, and not Sundays."

walk.text:
He looks at your boots for about a second and a half.

"Outside edge," he says. "Both. More on the left. And you're coming down heavy on the heel, which is the road out there rather than anything you're doing."

He goes back to the bench.

"That's not a fault, it's just what you do, and a heel built square for somebody who walks like that is a heel that's wrong in a fortnight. So I build it to the wear. That's all the trade is, really. Everybody thinks it's the sewing."

options.label: What can you tell from my boots?

root.text: "Sit down if you're stopping." He does not look up. "Boots on the bench and I'll do them while you watch. That's what the chair's for."

text_by_relation.familiar:
He looks at your boots before he looks at you, and nods at the chair.

"Sit down," he says. "Let's see what you've done to them."
text_by_relation.first:
A narrow man on a stool glances at your feet before he glances at your face, which turns out to be the order he does everything in.

"Oswin Trapnell." Three tacks in his lips make it sound like less of a name than it is. "Soles, heels, welts."

He drives a tack, flat, one blow.

"Bring me both of them. Never one. And there's a chair, and it faces this way on purpose."
text_by_relation.known: "Ah." He does not look up. "What's coming apart?"

clothing_layers: a canvas apron gone black and shiny across the lap
a collarless shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow
corduroy trousers and, in the shop, no shoes at all

name: Oswin Trapnell
